front: raise NewError(...) from err - what does it do?
back: Chains err as the new exception's __cause__, so the traceback shows the low-level root cause under 'the direct cause of' your domain error. Raising without 'from' loses or muddles the root cause.

Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission: try the operation and catch the specific exception, instead of pre-checking conditions (Look Before You Leap). Pythonic because pre-checks race and duplicate logic.

front: Why doesn't asyncio speed up CPU-bound code?
back: The event loop is one thread that only switches at await points; CPU work never yields, so nothing overlaps and everything else stalls behind it. Async overlaps waiting, not computing - use processes for CPU.

front: Validate at the boundary - the principle?
back: Parse and validate untrusted input once at the edge (Pydantic), then pass typed, trusted objects internally (dataclasses). Inside the boundary, types are guarantees, not hopes.

front: Mocking rule: where do you patch?
back: Where the name is USED, not where it's defined: patch myapp.fetcher.get, not httpx.get, because the module under test holds its own reference. Patching the wrong path gives green tests and broken prod.
401 Unauthorized: not authenticated - 'who are you?'. 403 Forbidden: authenticated but not allowed - 'I know who you are, and no'.

front: Which status code for rate limiting, and which header goes with it?
back: 429 Too Many Requests, with a Retry-After header saying when to come back. Well-behaved clients honor it and back off with jitter.

front: Idempotent method - definition, and which HTTP methods qualify?
back: Repeating the request has the same effect as sending it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by contract; POST is not - which is why retrying a create needs an idempotency key.

Client sends a unique key per logical operation in a header; the server stores the first response under that key and replays it for any retry instead of re-executing. Same key + different payload = 409.
Verify the HMAC signature with the shared secret, reject stale timestamps (replay window), dedupe by event id, respond 2xx fast and enqueue the real processing for a worker.

front: What does TTFT measure, and why does it matter?
back: Time to first token - how long the user stares at nothing. Streaming makes an 8-second answer feel fast because TTFT is sub-second; track p95 TTFT and total latency as separate metrics.
0 for extraction, classification and eval runs - near-deterministic sampling. Around 1 for ideation and varied prose. It scales randomness; it does not make facts more correct.

front: Cache breakpoints: what goes before one, and what's the pricing shape?
back: The long byte-stable prefix (system contract, tool defs, shared context) goes before the breakpoint; volatile content after. Cache writes cost a premium (~1.25x input), reads ~0.1x - so it pays when the prefix repeats within the TTL.

front: Context window: what counts against it?
back: Input AND output tokens share the one budget. Overflow means truncation or a hard error - and even inside the limit, long context costs linearly in money and latency.

front: Cost of one LLM call - the formula?
back: (input_tokens / 1M x input_price) + (output_tokens / 1M x output_price). Example: 3k in at $3/M plus 300 out at $15/M is about 1.4 cents.
So a fact spanning a boundary ('revenue grew' / '23% in Q3') survives intact in at least one chunk. A little index redundancy buys unbroken facts at retrieval time.
Answer only from the provided context, cite sources, and say so when the context doesn't contain the answer. An honest refusal beats a confident hallucination in any enterprise setting.
Merge multiple rankings by scoring each document with the sum of 1/(k + rank) across lists (k commonly 60). Lets you fuse BM25 and vector results without comparing incompatible score scales.
Models attend best to the start and end of a long context; facts buried mid-context get missed. Pack the highest-value chunks at the edges and resist stuffing k=20 into the prompt.

front: Why keep BM25 alongside vector search?
back: Embeddings miss exact terms - ticker codes, part numbers, names, negation. BM25 nails exact-match queries, vectors handle paraphrase; hybrid with RRF covers both query types.

front: Cosine similarity - what does it measure?
back: The angle between vectors, ignoring magnitude: 1 = same direction, ~0 = unrelated. On L2-normalized vectors it equals the dot product - hence: normalize once, then use fast dot products.
'Profits rose' and 'profits fell' embed suspiciously close: similar topic, opposite meaning. Embedding similarity is topical, not logical - hybrid search and reranking pick up the slack.
Hierarchical Navigable Small World - a layered graph index for approximate nearest-neighbour search. Trades a sliver of exact recall for sub-linear query time at millions of vectors.

Bi-encoder embeds query and document separately: fast, indexable, coarse. Cross-encoder scores the pair together: slow, precise. Pattern: retrieve ~20 wide with the first, rerank to ~5 sharp with the second.

front: Can you mix embedding models in one index?
back: No - different models produce unrelated vector spaces, even at the same dimension, so similarities become noise. A model upgrade means re-embed the whole corpus, version the index, cut over, invalidate caches.
Model returns tool_use (name + args) -> your code validates and executes -> append tool_result -> call the model again -> repeat until it stops with text. The model only ever asks; your code acts.

front: Workflow vs agent - the one-line criteria?
back: Steps known in advance: workflow (predictable, cheap, debuggable). Steps genuinely dynamic AND progress verifiable AND the cost tolerable: maybe an agent. Most products are better as workflows.
...the model's only manual. Write them like API docs: what it does, when to use it, argument constraints (enums where possible), and what it returns - including an honest not_found result.

max_steps, a per-run cost cap, repeated-identical-call detection, a tool allowlist, Pydantic validation of arguments before execution, and a full transcript log - the transcript is both debugger and resumable state.
Pause before consequential actions (write, send, delete, spend): show the human the concrete plan or diff, take approve/deny - and feed a denial's reason back to the model so it can replan.
The fraction of gold queries for which at least one expected source appears in the top 5 retrieved chunks. It answers: did retrieval find the right material at all?
Mean Reciprocal Rank: the average of 1/rank of the first correct result across queries. recall@k says whether the right chunk is present; MRR says how high it lands.

Position bias (favors the first answer), verbosity bias (longer reads as better), self-preference (favors its own style) - plus sycophancy toward confident tone. Rubrics, evidence quotes and calibration are the antidotes.

front: How does a judge earn your trust?
back: Calibration: hand-label 10-20 outputs first, run the judge on the same set, measure agreement. Only once judge and human labels align do its unsupervised scores mean anything.

Groundedness: is every claim supported by the retrieved context? Correctness: does the answer match gold? An answer can be grounded but incomplete, or correct by luck while ungrounded - score them separately.

front: SETNX - what is it and what's it for?
back: Redis SET with NX (only if the key doesn't exist) plus EX for expiry - one atomic operation. The primitive behind idempotency guards, job dedupe and simple distributed locks.
On read: check the cache; on miss, compute from the source of truth and write back with a TTL. The application owns the logic - the cache is a look-aside accelerator, never the source of truth.
The key must encode everything the value depends on - model, prompt version, normalized query, index version, tenant. Any dependency you omit becomes a stale-answer bug later.
One query for N rows, then one more per row inside a loop - usually ORM lazy loading. The tell: N near-identical queries in the log. Fix with eager loading (selectinload/joinedload) or a join.
...every job can run twice, so jobs must be idempotent: dedupe with a content-hash SETNX guard, check-before-work, upsert instead of insert. Exactly-once delivery is marketing.
Latency, traffic, errors, saturation. For an LLM service: p95 TTFT and total, tokens per minute, refusal and malformed-output rates, queue depth and provider rate-limit headroom.

front: Circuit breaker: three states and transitions?
back: Closed (calls flow, failures counted) -> Open when the threshold trips (fail fast, no calls) -> Half-open after a cooldown (probe requests: success closes it, failure re-opens). Stops you hammering a struggling dependency.
The caller's deadline bounds everything inside: each inner timeout must be shorter than the outer one, with retry headroom included, or you burn work for clients that already gave up.

front: Top discovery questions before proposing an AI system?
back: Who uses it, how often? What does the current process cost, and what does a failure cost? Where does the data live, how fresh is it, who may access it? What number defines success? Which compliance constraints apply?

front: ROI framing for an AI proposal?
back: Value = hours saved x loaded cost + errors avoided x failure cost, set against system cost: tokens, infra, people, maintenance. Present ranges with named assumptions, and define the POC metric that would prove the value.

front: Jitter: why add randomness to backoff?
back: Synchronized clients retry in waves that re-spike the recovering dependency - the thundering herd. Randomized delays spread the retries out so recovery can actually happen.
One id generated at the edge and propagated through headers, log lines AND job payloads, so a single request's journey across API, queue and workers can be reconstructed with one search.

front: Why p95 latency instead of the mean?
back: The mean hides tail pain: nine fast requests and one 30-second hang average out to 'fine'. p95/p99 describe what your slowest real users actually experience - and LLM latency tails are long.

front: Symptom of a blocked event loop?
back: Everything goes serial: unrelated endpoints slow down together and concurrency collapses to one. Cause: sync work (time.sleep, requests, heavy CPU) inside async def. Fix: async equivalents, or push it to a thread.
Machines read logs: JSON fields like request_id, duration_ms and cost are queryable and aggregatable, where prose needs regex archaeology. Log events with fields, not sentences.

Malicious instructions hidden in content your system ingests - retrieved docs, tool results, inbound email - that fire when a model reads them. The attacker never touches your app, only your data sources.

front: OWASP LLM Top 10 - name three items.
back: LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM06 Excessive Agency. Use the full list as a pre-launch review checklist against your architecture.

front: Tenant isolation - where is it enforced?
back: At the data layer: tenant_id on every table, vector payload and cache key, applied as a mandatory filter in the retriever and queries. Proven by a permanent test: user A can never retrieve user B's documents.

front: Why is 'the prompt forbids it' not a security control?
back: Prompts are advisory, probabilistic and injectable - they share a channel with attacker content. Enforcement belongs in code and queries; the model should never see data it isn't allowed to leak.

front: Secrets hygiene for an LLM service?
back: Env vars or a secret manager only - never code, logs or third-party prompts; constant-time comparison for API keys; rotation-ready; and a CI grep-audit so a leaked key fails the build.

Each instruction is a cached layer, invalidated top-down when its inputs change. Copy dependency manifests and install first, copy code last - then a code edit rebuilds seconds of layers, not the whole image.
Build with the fat tooling in one stage, copy only the app and its venv into a slim runtime stage. Smaller, faster-pulling image with less attack surface - and run it as a non-root USER.

front: CI gates for an AI service?
back: Lint (ruff), offline tests with mocked LLM fixtures, an image build, plus a small eval smoke (about 5 cases, temperature 0, spend cap) - all required checks behind branch protection. The full eval set runs pre-release, not per PR.

front: What is a health check's job in deployment?
back: It gates traffic: compose won't start dependents and a PaaS won't cut over until it passes, so a broken build never replaces a working one. Point it at real readiness, not just process-up.
Config lives in environment variables, not code: one immutable image runs in every environment, secrets stay out of the repo, and rollback is just redeploying the previous image.
